title: A Cheaper House Can Still Mean a Bigger Mortgage Payment
text:
A house-price headline tells a buyer how much to borrow, but not how hard the loan will be to repay. How did the income burden of financing a new U.S. home change between 2019 and 2024, and how much does the interest rate matter? This matters for first-time buyers: falling prices can coexist with expensive financing, while existing owners may retain an earlier, cheaper mortgage.
I combine three public FRED series: Census/HUD new-home sale prices, Freddie Mac’s 30-year mortgage rate, and Census median household income. This is a new aggregate housing dataset, separate from the CPS microdata used in my previous post. The window ends in 2024 to compare six complete calendar years consistently.

title: A Cheaper House Can Still Mean a Bigger Mortgage Payment
section: Turning three series into one comparison
text:
Turning three series into one comparison
I average the four quarterly price medians and the weekly mortgage rates within each year, then merge these with that year’s household income. Averaging quarterly medians produces a price proxy, not the annual median transaction price. All calculations use the included CSV snapshots; a separate R script downloads the same series directly from FRED without an API key.
The hypothetical buyer puts 20% down and takes a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage. The standard amortization formula converts the remaining 80% into a monthly principal-and-interest payment. Dividing that payment by annual gross income divided by twelve gives a comparable burden measure. Both money amounts refer to the same year: a common inflation deflator would cancel in their ratio. These are scenario calculations at annual-average inputs, not observed household payments.

title: A Cheaper House Can Still Mean a Bigger Mortgage Payment
text:
Prices moved ahead of incomes





Figure 1. Annual new-home price proxy and median household income, indexed to 2019 = 100.




Figure 1 puts both series at 100 in 2019, making their percentage changes comparable. By 2024, prices were 30.8% higher, while income was 21% higher. The price-to-income ratio rose from 4.66 to 5.04. Buyers therefore needed a larger loan relative to income even before considering interest. The price proxy fell 3.2% between 2022 and 2024, but this alone did not restore the earlier financing burden.

title: A Cheaper House Can Still Mean a Bigger Mortgage Payment
text:
The low-rate cushion disappeared





Figure 2. Annual arithmetic mean of Freddie Mac’s weekly 30-year fixed mortgage rates.




Figure 2 explains the missing piece. The annual-average mortgage rate fell from 3.94% in 2019 to 2.96% in 2021, then reached 6.81% in 2023. Lower rates initially cushioned rising prices by reducing the cost of financing each borrowed dollar. That cushion reversed. In 2024, the rate remained 6.72%, so a slightly cheaper house could still require a much larger payment than before the pandemic.

title: A Cheaper House Can Still Mean a Bigger Mortgage Payment
text:
Combining the two pressures





Figure 3. Illustrative mortgage principal and interest as a percentage of median gross household income. The dashed line fixes the rate at its 2019 average while retaining each year’s price and income.




Figure 3 translates prices and rates into the same economic unit: a share of income. The payment increased from $1,214 to $2,168 per month, a 78.6% increase. Its income share rose from 21.2% to 31.3%, an increase of 10.1 percentage points.
Holding the rate at its 2019 average gives a 2024 burden of 22.9%, or 8.4 percentage points below the observed-rate scenario. This isolates financing arithmetic while keeping price and income unchanged. It is not a causal estimate: different rates could also change prices, construction, and who buys.

title: A Cheaper House Can Still Mean a Bigger Mortgage Payment
text:
Sources and limits
The downloadable inputs are MSPUS, MORTGAGE30US, and MEHOINUSA646N, retrieved October 5, 2026. Freddie Mac changed its survey methodology in November 2022. National new-home prices do not describe existing homes or local markets, and all-household median income does not represent the median buyer. Taxes, insurance, closing costs, maintenance, and savings constraints are excluded. The repository includes raw CSVs, readable R scripts, generated figures and tables, and replication instructions.

title: A Cheaper House Can Still Mean a Bigger Mortgage Payment
text:
Takeaway
A cheaper purchase price does not necessarily mean an affordable payment. After 2019, higher prices relative to income and higher financing costs jointly raised this illustrative burden. Buyers should compare the loan’s payment with their own income and total ownership costs, rather than treating a decline in national house prices as proof that affordability has recovered.


View the complete R analysis and visualization code



Code
# Blog Post 4: housing prices, mortgage rates, and household income.
# Only ggplot2 is needed beyond base R. No API key is required.
# From the website root:
#   post_dir <- "blog/posts/post4"
#   source(file.path(post_dir, "R", "analysis.R"))

library(ggplot2)
if (!exists("post_dir")) post_dir <- "."

raw_dir <- file.path(post_dir, "data", "raw")
processed_dir <- file.path(post_dir, "data", "processed")
results_dir <- file.path(post_dir, "results")
dir.create(processed_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(results_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# 1. Read the three included FRED CSV snapshots.
# A period marks a missing FRED observation; treat it as NA, not zero.
prices <- read.csv(file.path(raw_dir, "MSPUS.csv"), na.strings = c(".", ""))
rates <- read.csv(file.path(raw_dir, "MORTGAGE30US.csv"), na.strings = c(".", ""))
income <- read.csv(file.path(raw_dir, "MEHOINUSA646N.csv"), na.strings = c(".", ""))

# FRED sometimes calls its first column DATE instead of observation_date.
# Use the first column for dates and the documented series ID for values.
prices$year <- as.integer(substr(prices[[1]], 1, 4))
rates$year <- as.integer(substr(rates[[1]], 1, 4))
income$year <- as.integer(substr(income[[1]], 1, 4))
prices$MSPUS <- as.numeric(prices$MSPUS)
rates$MORTGAGE30US <- as.numeric(rates$MORTGAGE30US)
income$MEHOINUSA646N <- as.numeric(income$MEHOINUSA646N)

years <- 2019:2024
prices <- prices[prices$year %in% years, ]
rates <- rates[rates$year %in% years, ]
income <- income[income$year %in% years, ]

# Require complete annual inputs rather than filling in missing observations.
# There must be four quarterly prices and 52 or 53 weekly rates each year.
for (year in years) {
  p <- prices$MSPUS[prices$year == year]
  r <- rates$MORTGAGE30US[rates$year == year]
  y <- income$MEHOINUSA646N[income$year == year]
  stopifnot(length(p) == 4, all(is.finite(p)), all(p > 0))
  stopifnot(length(r) >= 52, length(r) <= 53, all(is.finite(r)), all(r > 0))
  stopifnot(length(y) == 1, is.finite(y), y > 0)
}

# 2. Put each input on an annual calendar-year basis.
# The mean of four quarterly medians is a price proxy, NOT an annual median.
# Weekly interest rates receive equal weight in the annual mean.
annual_prices <- aggregate(MSPUS ~ year, data = prices, FUN = mean)
annual_rates <- aggregate(MORTGAGE30US ~ year, data = rates, FUN = mean)
annual_income <- income[, c("year", "MEHOINUSA646N")]

housing <- merge(annual_prices, annual_rates, by = "year")
housing <- merge(housing, annual_income, by = "year")
names(housing) <- c("year", "price_usd", "rate_pct", "income_usd")
housing <- housing[order(housing$year), ]
stopifnot(identical(housing$year, years))

# 3. Construct comparable indexes and a transparent mortgage calculation.
base <- housing[housing$year == 2019, ]
last <- housing[housing$year == 2024, ]
housing$price_index <- 100 * housing$price_usd / base$price_usd
housing$income_index <- 100 * housing$income_usd / base$income_usd
housing$price_to_income <- housing$price_usd / housing$income_usd

# Assumptions: 20% down, 30-year fixed mortgage, 360 monthly payments.
# P&I = L * m / (1 - (1 + m)^(-360)), where m is the monthly rate.
# This is a payment at annual-average inputs, not an average borrower payment.
housing$loan_usd <- 0.80 * housing$price_usd
monthly_rate <- housing$rate_pct / 100 / 12
housing$monthly_pi_usd <- housing$loan_usd * monthly_rate /
  (1 - (1 + monthly_rate)^(-360))
housing$payment_share_pct <- 100 * 12 * housing$monthly_pi_usd / housing$income_usd

# Mechanical comparison: retain each year's price and income, fix the rate.
# This does not predict how prices would react to different interest rates.
fixed_rate <- base$rate_pct / 100 / 12
housing$monthly_pi_fixed_rate_usd <- housing$loan_usd * fixed_rate /
  (1 - (1 + fixed_rate)^(-360))
housing$payment_share_fixed_rate_pct <-
  100 * 12 * housing$monthly_pi_fixed_rate_usd / housing$income_usd
housing$down_payment_share_pct <- 100 * 0.20 * housing$price_usd / housing$income_usd

# Both payments and income are nominal dollars from the same calendar year.
# A common price deflator cancels in their ratio: (payment/CPI)/(income/CPI).
write.csv(housing, file.path(processed_dir, "housing_annual.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# 4. Prepare the plotting tables without pivoting, nested lists, or joins.
index_data <- rbind(
  data.frame(year = housing$year, series = "New-home price", value = housing$price_index),
  data.frame(year = housing$year, series = "Household income", value = housing$income_index)
)
burden_data <- rbind(
  data.frame(year = housing$year, series = "Observed annual-average rate",
             value = housing$payment_share_pct),
  data.frame(year = housing$year, series = "Rate held at its 2019 average",
             value = housing$payment_share_fixed_rate_pct)
)
index_labels <- index_data[index_data$year == 2024, ]
index_labels$label <- paste0(round(index_labels$value, 1))
burden_labels <- burden_data[burden_data$year == 2024, ]
burden_labels$label <- paste0(round(burden_labels$value, 1), "%")
rate_labels <- housing[housing$year %in% c(2019, 2021, 2023, 2024), ]
rate_labels$label <- paste0(round(rate_labels$rate_pct, 2), "%")

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))
common_theme <- theme(
  plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 18, color = "#17324D"),
  plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "#45596B"),
  plot.caption = element_text(size = 9, color = "#52616D", hjust = 0),
  panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
  panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
  legend.position = "top", legend.title = element_blank(),
  plot.margin = margin(12, 20, 12, 12)
)

plot_1 <- ggplot(index_data, aes(x = year, y = value, color = series)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, color = "#ADB7BF", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) + geom_point(size = 2.8) +
  geom_text(data = index_labels, aes(label = label), hjust = -0.25,
            show.legend = FALSE, size = 4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("New-home price" = "#B65029", "Household income" = "#176B87")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = years, limits = c(2019, 2024.65)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(100, 140, 10), limits = c(97, 140)) +
  labs(title = "New-home prices outpaced household income after 2019",
       subtitle = "Annual summaries in current dollars; both series indexed to 2019 = 100",
       x = NULL, y = "Index (2019 = 100)",
       caption = "Sources: Census/HUD (MSPUS) and Census (MEHOINUSA646N), via FRED.\nPrice = unweighted mean of four quarterly medians; income = annual household median.") +
  common_theme

plot_2 <- ggplot(housing, aes(x = year, y = rate_pct)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, color = "#176B87") +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "#176B87") +
  geom_text(data = rate_labels, aes(label = label), vjust = -0.9,
            color = "#17324D", size = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = years) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 8), breaks = seq(0, 8, 2)) +
  labs(title = "The low-rate cushion disappeared",
       subtitle = "30-year fixed mortgage rate; simple average of weekly observations in each year",
       x = NULL, y = "Annual-average mortgage rate (%)",
       caption = "Source: Freddie Mac, MORTGAGE30US, via FRED. Copyright Freddie Mac; citation required.\nFreddie Mac changed its survey methodology on November 17, 2022.") +
  common_theme

plot_3 <- ggplot(burden_data, aes(x = year, y = value, color = series, linetype = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) + geom_point(size = 2.8) +
  geom_text(data = burden_labels, aes(label = label), hjust = -0.25,
            show.legend = FALSE, size = 4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Observed annual-average rate" = "#B65029",
                                "Rate held at its 2019 average" = "#176B87")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Observed annual-average rate" = "solid",
                                   "Rate held at its 2019 average" = "dashed")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = years, limits = c(2019, 2024.65)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 38), breaks = seq(0, 35, 5)) +
  labs(title = "The payment burden rose much more than the price ratio",
       subtitle = "Illustrative monthly principal and interest / monthly median gross household income",
       x = NULL, y = "Payment as a share of gross income (%)",
       caption = "Sources: Census/HUD and Freddie Mac, via FRED; author's calculation.\n20% down; 360 payments. Excludes taxes, insurance, fees, and maintenance; fixed-rate line holds price and income observed.") +
  common_theme

# 5. Save the figures and the numeric statements used in the article.
ggsave(file.path(results_dir, "01_price_and_income.png"), plot_1,
       width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 180, bg = "white")
ggsave(file.path(results_dir, "02_mortgage_rate.png"), plot_2,
       width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 180, bg = "white")
ggsave(file.path(results_dir, "03_payment_burden.png"), plot_3,
       width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 180, bg = "white")

# These objects supply inline R expressions in index.qmd.
base <- housing[housing$year == 2019, ]
last <- housing[housing$year == 2024, ]
low <- housing[housing$year == 2021, ]
peak <- housing[housing$year == 2023, ]
price_growth <- 100 * (last$price_usd / base$price_usd - 1)
income_growth <- 100 * (last$income_usd / base$income_usd - 1)
payment_growth <- 100 * (last$monthly_pi_usd / base$monthly_pi_usd - 1)
burden_change <- last$payment_share_pct - base$payment_share_pct
rate_gap <- last$payment_share_pct - last$payment_share_fixed_rate_pct
price_drop <- 100 * (last$price_usd / housing$price_usd[housing$year == 2022] - 1)

findings <- data.frame(
  statistic = c("2019_to_2024_price_growth_pct", "2019_to_2024_income_growth_pct",
                "2019_to_2024_monthly_payment_growth_pct", "payment_share_change_pp",
                "2024_fixed_2019_rate_gap_pp", "2022_to_2024_price_change_pct"),
  value = c(price_growth, income_growth, payment_growth, burden_change, rate_gap, price_drop)
)
write.csv(findings, file.path(results_dir, "key_findings.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(index_data, file.path(results_dir, "figure_1_data.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(housing[, c("year", "rate_pct")], file.path(results_dir, "figure_2_data.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(burden_data, file.path(results_dir, "figure_3_data.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

title: Where Should an Economics Student Start the Job Search?
text:
An economics student opens a job site. Should the first saved search be “economist,” “financial analyst,” or “data scientist”? Each can involve quantitative work, but choosing where to look requires more than finding a familiar title. Which occupations offer a useful starting point when weighing pay, growth, and the volume of openings?
I use R’s rvest package to extract six deliberately selected Bureau of Labor Statistics occupational profiles. They help compare job markets. They cannot show which occupation an economics graduate is most likely to enter.

title: Beyond the Economist Job Title: Where Should a Quantitative Student Look?
text:
An economics degree does not require a job with “economist” in its title. For a student with quantitative training, data science, operations research, finance, consulting, and market research are also plausible directions. But searching every category equally takes time. Which paths deserve attention when balancing earnings, growth, and the scale of opportunities?
I compare six deliberately selected occupations in the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Occupational Outlook Handbook. These are relevant alternatives, not a representative sample of every graduate career. The aim is to build a practical search shortlist rather than predict an individual’s employment outcome.

title: Beyond the Economist Job Title: Where Should a Quantitative Student Look?
section: From web pages to comparable data
text:
From web pages to comparable data
The project uses R’s rvest package to extract each page’s Quick Facts table and the Summary paragraph reporting average annual openings. The archived HTML was captured from the public pages in a browser on September 20, 2026. read_html(), html_elements(), and html_text2() turn those saved pages into structured observations. An optional collection function downloads fresh pages and applies the same extractor.
Cleaning removes excess whitespace, dollar signs, commas, and descriptive text attached to percentages. It keeps annual pay separate from hourly pay and checks for missing fields, duplicate occupations, and inconsistent reference years. The comparison uses May 2025 wages and 2025-2035 projections; retrieval date and measurement year are different concepts.
The pages require no login or paywall. The reviewed robots.txt does not disallow these occupation paths. Collection is limited to six profiles, with pauses between page requests. The refresh function checks current rules, stops on access errors, and never attempts to bypass restrictions. Reusing saved HTML avoids repeat requests during editing.

title: Beyond the Economist Job Title: Where Should a Quantitative Student Look?
section: Growth is not the same as opportunity volume
text:
Growth is not the same as opportunity volume
Data scientists have the fastest projected growth: 35%, compared with 5% for economists. Their median annual pay is $120,230, only $4,490 below economists’ $124,720. For a student interested in both economic questions and computation, this makes data science a compelling direction to investigate.
However, the annual-openings ranking tells a different story. Management analysts have approximately 94,100 openings, market research analysts 82,000, and data scientists 24,800. Economists have 1,100. Data science therefore has about 22.5 times as many projected annual openings as economics, despite a similar median wage.
These measures answer different questions. Growth describes the percentage increase in employment over a decade. Openings include positions arising when workers leave an occupation or retire, as well as expansion. A large, slower-growing occupation can consequently generate more openings than a small, fast-growing one.





Figure 1. Growth identifies expanding fields, not the number of available positions.









Figure 2. The largest projected opening counts belong to different occupations than the fastest growth.

title: Beyond the Economist Job Title: Where Should a Quantitative Student Look?
section: Turning the comparison into a search strategy
text:
Turning the comparison into a search strategy
For a transparent starting rule, I screen for a median wage of at least USD 85,000, projected growth of at least 10%, and no typical requirement for related work experience. These thresholds express a hypothetical student’s preferences; they are not official quality ratings. Data scientists and operations research analysts pass this screen. Operations research offers 12% growth, $88,940 median pay, and approximately 7,500 annual openings.
The recommendation is to make these two categories regular saved searches, while retaining market research and financial analysis as alternatives for applicants whose interests fit them. Management analysis has the most openings, but its typical related-experience requirement means a new graduate should specifically look for entry-level or campus programs. Economics remains attractive for students committed to economic research, but searching only that title would unnecessarily narrow the opportunity set.
The shortlist depends on preferences. Raising the wage threshold to USD 90,000, or the growth threshold to 15%, removes operations research in this snapshot. The code saves a nine-scenario sensitivity table so readers can inspect how changing the rule changes the recommendation.

title: Beyond the Economist Job Title: Where Should a Quantitative Student Look?
text:
Limits and takeaway
Median wages cover workers at different career stages; they are not starting salaries. Projected openings are not current vacancies, internships, or evidence of low competition. National averages hide geographic differences, and these profiles cannot establish employer-specific skills, work-authorization eligibility, or an applicant’s probability of receiving an offer. Financial analysts also combine multiple specialties; this comparison consistently uses the combined Quick Facts figures.
The actionable takeaway is to broaden the search beyond “economist,” prioritize data science and operations research under the stated preferences, and evaluate individual postings before applying. Web scraping becomes useful when comparable information changes a decision, with its limitations kept visible.

# Collect structured information from BLS HTML using rvest.
# Run from the project root. Archived HTML makes the default run reproducible.
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(rvest)
  library(dplyr)
  library(stringr)
  library(readr)
})

sources <- tibble::tribble(
  ~id, ~occupation, ~path,
  "data-scientists", "Data scientists", "math/data-scientists.htm",
  "economists", "Economists", "life-physical-and-social-science/economists.htm",
  "operations-research-analysts", "Operations research analysts", "math/operations-research-analysts.htm",
  "market-research-analysts", "Market research analysts", "business-and-financial/market-research-analysts.htm",
  "management-analysts", "Management analysts", "business-and-financial/management-analysts.htm",
  "financial-analysts", "Financial analysts", "business-and-financial/financial-analysts.htm"
) |>
  mutate(url = paste0("https://www.bls.gov/ooh/", path))

scrape_profile <- function(file, id, occupation, url) {
  page <- read_html(file, encoding = "UTF-8")
  rows <- html_elements(page, "#quickfacts tbody tr")
  if (length(rows) != 7L) stop("Quick Facts structure changed: ", file)
  fields <- tibble::tibble(
    label = str_squish(html_text2(html_element(rows, "th"))),
    value = str_squish(html_text2(html_element(rows, "td")))
  )
  get_field <- function(pattern) {
    value <- fields$value[str_detect(fields$label, regex(pattern, ignore_case = TRUE))]
    if (length(value) != 1L || is.na(value) || value == "") {
      stop("Missing or ambiguous field: ", pattern, " in ", file)
    }
    value
  }
  # Scope to the Summary article, so the same sentence elsewhere is not counted twice.
  summary <- html_element(page, "article[aria-labelledby='Summary']")
  if (is.na(html_name(summary))) stop("Summary article missing: ", file)
  body <- str_squish(html_text2(summary))
  openings <- str_match(body, "About\\s+([0-9,]+)\\s+openings")[, 2]
  period <- str_match(body, "from\\s+(20[0-9]{2})\\s+to\\s+(20[0-9]{2})")
  pay_label <- fields$label[str_detect(fields$label, "Median Pay")]
  pay_text <- get_field("Median Pay")
  result <- tibble::tibble(
    id, occupation, source_url = url,
    # Annual pay is the FIRST amount; the hourly amount is deliberately excluded.
    median_pay_usd = parse_number(pay_text),
    pay_year = as.integer(str_extract(pay_label, "20[0-9]{2}")),
    education = get_field("Entry-Level Education"),
    experience = get_field("Work Experience"),
    employment = parse_number(get_field("Number of Jobs")),

refresh_sources <- function(destination = "data/live") {
  if (!requireNamespace("httr2", quietly = TRUE)) stop("Install httr2 first.")
  if (dir.exists(destination)) stop("Use a new destination to preserve earlier data.")
  ua <- "EconomicsCourseProject/1.0 (six public BLS career pages; educational use)"
  get_public <- function(url) {
    httr2::request(url) |>
      httr2::req_user_agent(ua) |>
      httr2::req_timeout(30) |>
      httr2::req_perform()  # Stops on HTTP errors, including 403 and 429. No retries.
  }
  robots <- httr2::resp_body_string(get_public("https://www.bls.gov/robots.txt"))
  if (!grepl("User-agent:", robots, ignore.case = TRUE)) stop("Cannot verify robots.txt.")
  # Conservative check: honor Disallow rules from ALL groups, ignore Allow
  # exceptions, and stop if any rule could exclude one of these six paths.
  # This intentionally may refuse more than necessary; it never tries to evade a rule.
  lines <- trimws(gsub("#.*$", "", strsplit(robots, "\n", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]))
  rules <- trimws(sub("^[Dd]isallow\\s*:", "", lines[grepl("^[Dd]isallow\\s*:", lines)]))
  rules <- rules[nzchar(rules)]
  url_paths <- sub("https://www.bls.gov", "", sources$url, fixed = TRUE)
  for (rule in rules) {
    # Convert robots wildcards to a regular expression. Unanchored rules
    # match prefixes; a terminal $ requires a match through the end of a path.
    pattern <- glob2rx(sub("\\$$", "", rule), trim.head = FALSE, trim.tail = FALSE)
    if (!endsWith(rule, "$")) pattern <- sub("\\$$", "", pattern)
    if (any(grepl(pattern, url_paths))) {
      stop("A robots.txt rule may disallow these pages: ", rule,
           ". Stop and review the site's policy; do not bypass it.")
    }
  }
  delay <- 3
  crawl <- lines[grepl("^Crawl-delay:", lines, ignore.case = TRUE)]
  if (length(crawl)) delay <- max(delay, parse_number(crawl), na.rm = TRUE)
  dir.create(destination, recursive = TRUE)
  writeLines(robots, file.path(destination, "robots.txt"))
  manifest <- list()
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(sources))) {
    Sys.sleep(delay)
    s <- sources[i, ]
    response <- get_public(s$url)
    content <- httr2::resp_body_raw(response)
    file <- file.path(destination, paste0(s$id, ".html"))
    writeBin(content, file)
    # rvest collects and validates the relevant fields immediately after download.
    scrape_profile(file, s$id, s$occupation, s$url)
    manifest[[i]] <- tibble::tibble(id = s$id, source_url = s$url,
      access_date = as.character(Sys.Date()), capture_method = "HTTP download; rvest extraction")
    write_csv(bind_rows(manifest), file.path(destination, "manifest.csv"))
  }
  message("Saved six pages. Run run_project(raw_dir = '", destination, "') to analyze them.")
  invisible(destination)
}

title: A P-Value of 0.03 Is Not a Funding Recommendation
text:
Imagine a city deciding whether to fund a job-training program. An evaluation reports higher wages and a p-value of 0.030. Does that mean a 97% chance the program works? And is it enough to justify spending public money?
The first answer is no. The second needs more information. The useful question is what this number tells a decision-maker, and what it leaves unanswered.
There is evidence that the probability interpretation causes difficulty. In a 2022 survey by Lytsy, Hartman, and Pingel, 53.3% of 75 doctoral students and 73.4% of 64 statisticians/epidemiologists interpreted a significant result as indicating that the null hypothesis was improbable. Those respondents do not establish how prevalent this interpretation is among all researchers or economists. They do provide a specific reason to examine it, rather than simply declaring that everyone gets p-values wrong.

title: Why a Small P-Value Does Not Mean Your Hypothesis Is Probably Wrong
text:
The p-value is one of the most commonly used—and commonly misunderstood—ideas in statistics. It appears everywhere from economics papers to medical studies, often as the number that determines whether a result is called “statistically significant.”
A common interpretation is that a p-value tells us the probability that the null hypothesis is true. For example, someone might say that a p-value of 0.03 means there is only a 3% chance that the null hypothesis is correct.
That interpretation is wrong.
A p-value instead answers a more specific question:

If the null hypothesis were true, how surprising would our observed data—or something even more extreme—be?

This difference sounds subtle, but it is extremely important.

title: Why a Small P-Value Does Not Mean Your Hypothesis Is Probably Wrong
text:
A Simple Example
Suppose an economist wants to study whether a job-training program increases workers’ wages.
The null hypothesis might be
\[H_0: \beta = 0,\]
where \(\beta\) represents the effect of the training program on wages.
The alternative hypothesis is
\[H_1: \beta \neq 0.\]
Imagine that the estimated effect is positive and produces a p-value of 0.03.
This does not mean
\[P(H_0 \mid \text{data}) = 0.03.\]
Instead, the p-value is closer to
\[P(\text{data at least this extreme} \mid H_0).\]
In words: assuming that the training program truly has no effect, there would be about a 3% chance of observing evidence at least as inconsistent with the null hypothesis as what we actually observed.

title: Why a Small P-Value Does Not Mean Your Hypothesis Is Probably Wrong
text:
Why Is This Unintuitive?
The confusion comes from reversing the direction of conditional probability.
What researchers often want to know is
\[P(H_0 \mid \text{data}),\]
the probability that the null hypothesis is true given the data.
But a traditional hypothesis test gives us information about
\[P(\text{data} \mid H_0),\]
the probability of observing the data assuming the null hypothesis is true.
These are not the same quantity.
Consider an analogy. Suppose that if a person has a rare disease, there is a 95% probability that a diagnostic test will be positive. This does not imply that someone who tests positive has a 95% probability of having the disease. We would also need to know how common the disease is and how often the test gives false positives.
The same logical issue appears when interpreting p-values.

title: Why a Small P-Value Does Not Mean Your Hypothesis Is Probably Wrong
text:
What Does “Statistically Significant” Mean?
Researchers often compare the p-value to a significance level such as
\[\alpha = 0.05.\]
If
\[p < 0.05,\]
the result is commonly described as statistically significant, and the null hypothesis is rejected.
However, the 0.05 threshold is a convention rather than a fundamental law of statistics. A result with a p-value of 0.049 is not fundamentally different from one with a p-value of 0.051.
Statistical significance also does not imply economic significance.
For example, a very large dataset might show that a training program increases wages by only $0.10 per year with a very small p-value. The effect could be statistically convincing while being economically meaningless.
Conversely, an economically important effect may fail to achieve statistical significance if the sample is small or noisy.

title: Why a Small P-Value Does Not Mean Your Hypothesis Is Probably Wrong
text:
The Main Lesson
A p-value should be viewed as a measure of how compatible the observed data are with a particular null hypothesis—not as the probability that the hypothesis is true.
When interpreting an empirical result, economists should therefore look beyond whether \(p < 0.05\). The estimated effect size, confidence interval, sample size, research design, and economic importance of the result are often just as important as the p-value itself.
Understanding this distinction makes hypothesis testing much less mysterious and helps prevent one of the most persistent statistical mistakes in applied research.

title: The College Earnings Premium Is Not One Number
text:
College is often discussed as if it produces one stable earnings return. That shorthand hides at least three dimensions: calendar time, differences between women and men, and workers’ position in the life cycle. How large is the bachelor’s earnings premium, and how does it vary along those dimensions?
I use IPUMS Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC) microdata. The analytic sample contains wage and salary workers ages 25–64 who worked at least 50 weeks and usually at least 35 hours per week. This full-time, full-year restriction reduces the role of differences in weeks and hours, although it also excludes people whose employment is less stable.
Annual wage income is divided by weeks worked to construct weekly earnings. CPI99 converts dollar values across years, and all results are expressed in 2024 dollars. Most importantly, every median is calculated with ASECWT, the IPUMS person-level weight for ASEC analysis. The figures therefore summarize the population represented by CPS rather than treating every sampled record as equally representative.

title: The College Earnings Premium Is Not One Number
section: The education hierarchy persisted, but its size changed
text:
The education hierarchy persisted, but its size changed





Figure 1. Weighted median real weekly earnings by education.




The first figure establishes the broad pattern. In every displayed year, median weekly earnings rise with educational attainment. For workers with a bachelor’s degree, the weighted median changed from $1,576 in 2000 to $1,577 in 2024. High-school graduates earned $962 at the median in the latest year.
Relative comparisons are often more informative than dollar gaps. The bachelor’s premium over high school moved from 60.3% to 64%, making it 3.7 percentage points wider across the displayed period. This is a descriptive contrast between groups—not the causal effect that the same person would experience from completing college.

title: The College Earnings Premium Is Not One Number
section: The premium is not identical for women and men
text:
The premium is not identical for women and men





Figure 2. Bachelor’s earnings premium relative to high-school graduates, by reported sex.




Figure 2 calculates the comparison separately using the CPS categories for female and male respondents. In 2024, the premium was 73.1% for women and 72.7% for men, so the relative education gap was larger among women. This does not mean that college eliminates the gender wage gap: each line compares bachelor’s and high-school workers within the same sex category. The pattern instead shows that the payoff associated with education can differ depending on the comparison group.

title: The College Earnings Premium Is Not One Number
text:
Earnings profiles diverge with age





Figure 3. Weighted median weekly earnings across age groups in the latest income year.




The cross-section by age supplies the final piece of the story. In 2024, the bachelor’s premium was 55.6% among workers ages 25–29 and 73.1% among those ages 50–54. These are not longitudinal careers: older and younger people belong to different cohorts, and CPS does not reveal what one worker’s earnings path will be. Still, the figure demonstrates why a single pooled premium can conceal economically meaningful life-cycle variation.

title: The College Earnings Premium Is Not One Number
text:
Takeaway and limitations
The central takeaway is that college graduates earn more at the weighted median, but the college earnings premium is not one universal number. It changes over time, differs between women and men, and varies across age groups. A student evaluating education should therefore ask which workers, which year, and which career stage underlie a quoted return.
The analysis remains descriptive. Education groups differ in occupation, field of study, experience, location, selection into employment, and other characteristics. Wage income excludes self-employment earnings; high incomes may be topcoded; population-control changes and sampling error can affect comparisons; and no confidence intervals are shown. These figures document patterns, not causal effects.

Data and reproducibility
Data are from IPUMS CPS, which harmonizes CPS microdata produced by the U.S. Census Bureau and Bureau of Labor Statistics. Variable definitions are documented for INCWAGE, WKSWORK1, UHRSWORKLY, and EDUC. IPUMS explains the appropriate CPS weights and CPI99 inflation adjustment.

find_ipums_extract <- function(raw_dir = "data/raw") {
  xml <- list.files(raw_dir, pattern = "\\.xml$", full.names = TRUE,
                    ignore.case = TRUE)
  data <- list.files(raw_dir, pattern = "\\.(dat|csv)\\.gz$", full.names = TRUE,
                     ignore.case = TRUE)

  if (length(xml) != 1 || length(data) != 1) {
    stop(
      "Place exactly one IPUMS DDI .xml file and its matching .dat.gz ",
      "(or .csv.gz) file in data/raw. See README.md."
    )
  }

  list(xml = xml, data = data)
}

classify_education <- function(x) {
  labels <- as.character(haven::as_factor(x, levels = "labels"))

  dplyr::case_when(
    stringr::str_detect(labels, stringr::regex(
      "high school (diploma|graduate)|GED|equivalent", ignore_case = TRUE
    )) ~ "High school",
    stringr::str_detect(labels, stringr::regex(
      "some college|associate", ignore_case = TRUE
    )) ~ "Some college / associate",
    stringr::str_detect(labels, stringr::regex(
      "bachelor", ignore_case = TRUE
    )) ~ "Bachelor's",
    stringr::str_detect(labels, stringr::regex(
      "master|professional school|doctor", ignore_case = TRUE
    )) ~ "Advanced degree",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  )
}

classify_sex <- function(x) {
  labels <- as.character(haven::as_factor(x, levels = "labels"))

  dplyr::case_when(
    stringr::str_detect(labels, stringr::regex("female", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Women",
    stringr::str_detect(labels, stringr::regex("male", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Men",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  )
}

load_and_prepare_cps <- function(raw_dir = "data/raw") {
  files <- find_ipums_extract(raw_dir)
  required <- c(
    "YEAR", "ASECWT", "AGE", "SEX", "EDUC", "INCWAGE", "WKSWORK1",
    "UHRSWORKLY"
  )

  cps <- ipumsr::read_ipums_micro(
    files$xml,
    vars = required,
    data_file = files$data,
    verbose = FALSE
  )
  names(cps) <- tolower(names(cps))

  missing <- setdiff(tolower(required), names(cps))
  if (length(missing) > 0) {
    stop("The IPUMS extract is missing: ", paste(toupper(missing), collapse = ", "))
  }

  cps <- cps |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      year = as.integer(year),
      income_year = year - 1L,
      education = classify_education(educ),
      sex_group = classify_sex(sex),
      age = as.numeric(age),
      asecwt = as.numeric(asecwt),
      incwage = as.numeric(incwage),
      wkswork1 = as.numeric(wkswork1),
      uhrsworkly = as.numeric(uhrsworkly)
    )

  # IPUMS CPS CPI99 factors convert prior-year income to constant 1999 dollars.
  # Keeping this small published lookup in the script avoids requiring CPI99 in
  # the user's extract. The selected ASEC years are documented in README.md.
  cpi99_lookup <- c(
    `2001` = 0.967,
    `2005` = 0.882,
    `2009` = 0.774,
    `2013` = 0.726,
    `2017` = 0.694,
    `2020` = 0.652,
    `2021` = 0.644,
    `2022` = 0.615,
    `2023` = 0.569,
    `2024` = 0.547,
    `2025` = 0.531
  )
  
  lookup_years <- as.integer(names(cpi99_lookup))
  
  # Only keep years covered by the documented inflation factors.
  ignored_years <- setdiff(sort(unique(cps$year)), lookup_years)
  if (length(ignored_years) > 0) {
    message("Ignoring years without a CPI99 factor: ",
            paste(ignored_years, collapse = ", "))
  }
  cps <- dplyr::filter(cps, year %in% lookup_years)
  cps$cpi99_factor <- unname(cpi99_lookup[match(cps$year, lookup_years)])

  prepared <- cps |>
    dplyr::filter(
      age >= 25, age <= 64,
      wkswork1 >= 50, wkswork1 <= 52,
      uhrsworkly >= 35, uhrsworkly < 999,
      incwage > 0, incwage < 99999999,
      is.finite(asecwt), asecwt > 0,
      !is.na(education), !is.na(sex_group),
      is.finite(cpi99_factor), cpi99_factor > 0
    ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      # CPI99 converts nominal income to 1999 dollars. Dividing by the
      # 2025-ASEC factor (0.531) converts 1999 dollars to 2024 dollars.
      weekly_earnings = incwage * cpi99_factor / 0.531 / wkswork1,
      education = factor(
        education,
        levels = c(
          "High school", "Some college / associate", "Bachelor's",
          "Advanced degree"
        )
      ),
      sex_group = factor(sex_group, levels = c("Women", "Men")),
      age_band = cut(
        age,
        breaks = c(25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 55, 60, 65),
        right = FALSE,
        labels = c(
          "25–29", "30–34", "35–39", "40–44",
          "45–49", "50–54", "55–59", "60–64"
        )
      )
    )

  if (nrow(prepared) == 0) {
    stop("No usable observations remain. Check the selected ASEC samples and variables.")
  }
  if (dplyr::n_distinct(prepared$income_year) < 3) {
    stop("Select at least three ASEC sample years; the README recommends eleven.")
  }
  if (!all(levels(prepared$education) %in% unique(as.character(prepared$education)))) {
    stop("Not all four education groups were found. Check EDUC labels in the extract.")
  }

  attr(prepared, "latest_dollar_year") <- 2024L
  prepared
}

weighted_median <- function(x, w) {
  keep <- is.finite(x) & is.finite(w) & w > 0
  x <- x[keep]
  w <- w[keep]
  if (length(x) == 0) return(NA_real_)

  ord <- order(x)
  x <- x[ord]
  w <- w[ord]
  x[which(cumsum(w) >= sum(w) / 2)[1]]
}

analyze_cps <- function(cps, results_dir = "results") {
  dir.create(results_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  dollar_year <- attr(cps, "latest_dollar_year")
  latest_year <- max(cps$income_year)

  trend <- weighted_summary(cps, income_year, education)

  overall_premium <- trend |>
    dplyr::filter(education %in% c("High school", "Bachelor's")) |>
    dplyr::select(income_year, education, median_weekly) |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = education, values_from = median_weekly) |>
    dplyr::mutate(

  by_sex <- weighted_summary(cps, income_year, sex_group, education)

title: A P-Value of 0.03 Is Not a Funding Recommendation
section: Imagine a world where the program does nothing
text:
Imagine a world where the program does nothing
Our example is hypothetical. Suppose a randomized evaluation estimates that training raises monthly wages by 20 dollars, with a standard error of 9.2 dollars. The standard error describes the estimate’s sampling uncertainty. Assume its sampling distribution is approximately normal with this known standard error; this simplified model lets us calculate the example directly in R.
The null hypothesis says that the true average wage effect is zero. Even in that no-effect world, repeated evaluations would produce different estimates because they observe different samples.
For a two-sided test, we count estimates at least as far from zero as the observed gain, in either direction. Here that means an estimate of at least +20 dollars or at most -20 dollars.






Figure 1: Normal sampling distribution of the estimated monthly wage effect under a zero-effect null. Both tails beyond minus and plus 20 dollars are shaded; together they contain approximately 3 percent of the probability.



R gives a probability of about 3.0% for those outcomes under the null model. That is the p-value. It is a probability about possible results assuming no effect, not a probability that no effect is true.

title: A P-Value of 0.03 Is Not a Funding Recommendation
text:
Why the direction matters
The reversal is tempting because we usually want the second answer: after seeing the evaluation, how likely is the program to work? But the test begins by assuming a zero effect, then evaluates the result against that assumption. It does not assign probabilities to the competing explanations.
Think of a fire alarm: knowing how often an alarm sounds when there is no fire does not, by itself, tell you the chance that a fire exists when it sounds. You also need information about actual fires and the alarm’s behavior during them. Likewise, a probability for the hypothesis requires additional assumptions and information, not simply subtracting the p-value from one.
The American Statistical Association’s 2016 guidance explicitly distinguishes p-values from probabilities that hypotheses are true, and advises against basing policy decisions solely on a significance threshold.

title: A P-Value of 0.03 Is Not a Funding Recommendation
text:
Significant, but worth funding?
Because 0.030 is below 0.05, the result would conventionally be called statistically significant. That tells us the estimate is relatively unusual under the specified no-effect model. It does not tell us the benefit is large.



Inputs and calculated results for the hypothetical training evaluation. All money amounts are monthly dollars per participant.

Now suppose the program costs 100 dollars per participant per month. The estimated wage gain is just 20 dollars. Its model-based 95% confidence interval runs from about 2 to 38 dollars. These results describe a positive but modest gain relative to the assumed cost.
This is not a complete benefit-cost analysis: effects might last beyond the evaluation, and training could produce benefits other than wages. The example nevertheless shows why crossing 0.05 cannot settle the funding decision.

title: A P-Value of 0.03 Is Not a Funding Recommendation
text:
What to ask next
For this evaluation, read the p-value alongside the estimated gain, uncertainty, study design, and program cost. The number answers how unusual the result would be under a no-effect model; deciding whether to fund the program requires a separate judgment about benefits and costs.






NoteSources and replication





The survey evidence comes from Lytsy, Hartman, and Pingel (2022), Upsala Journal of Medical Sciences, DOI 10.48101/ujms.v127.8760. Interpretive guidance comes from the ASA’s statement by Wasserstein and Lazar (2016), DOI 10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108. Both sources were accessed October 8, 2026.
All training-program amounts are invented teaching inputs, not estimates from an actual study. The normal approximation and known standard error are assumptions of this illustration. R/analysis.R reads data/example_inputs.csv and saves the figure, numeric results, plot data, and R session information to results/. The GitHub folder contains a README with replication instructions. No external data download or additional R analysis package is needed.

title: Where Should an Economics Student Start the Job Search?
section: A job category is not an academic background
text:
A job category is not an academic background
A financial analyst may have an economics degree, use economic models, and describe themselves as an economist. That does not make the BLS categories interchangeable. The Standard Occupational Classification assigns jobs according to work performed, with rules for mixed duties. Academic background and professional identity can cross those boundaries.
Here, “economists” means SOC 19-3011, while the financial-analysts profile combines 13-2051 (financial and investment analysts) and 13-2054 (financial risk specialists). The code records all component codes and checks that none appears in two comparison rows. Financial analysts’ combined statistics stay combined; a median cannot be split into subgroup medians.
These are occupational comparisons, not six exclusive groups of economics-trained people. I neither add the opening counts into a total for economics graduates nor interpret wage differences as the payoff from choosing one career over another.

title: Where Should an Economics Student Start the Job Search?
section: Fast growth and many openings tell different stories
text:
Fast growth and many openings tell different stories
In the archived profiles, data scientists lead projected growth at 35%, versus 5% for the economist occupation over 2025-2035. Their median annual pay, $120,230, is close to economists’ $124,720. That combination makes data science worth examining for a student who enjoys computation.





Projected employment growth by BLS occupational profile. Teal marks profiles passing the stated preference screen, not an official BLS rating.




The openings chart changes the emphasis. Management analysts have about 94,100 projected openings annually, market research analysts 82,000, and data scientists 24,800. The economist category has 1,100.
Growth measures expansion relative to an occupation’s existing size. Openings also include replacement needs when workers leave an occupation or retire. A large, slower-growing occupation can therefore generate more openings than a small, fast-growing one. These counts cover all qualifying workers, not positions reserved for economics graduates.





Projected average annual openings by BLS occupational profile. Counts include replacement needs and all experience levels; they are not current vacancies.

Suppose a student wants median pay of at least $85,000, projected growth of at least 10%, and no typical requirement for related work experience. title: Where Should an Economics Student Start the Job Search?
text:
What the comparison can—and cannot—decide
Median pay is not a starting salary. National projections do not reveal local vacancies, competition, visa eligibility, or an applicant’s hiring probability. The six profiles are a selected comparison, and their workers differ in skills and experience.
The takeaway is to use occupational evidence to choose searches, then use actual job descriptions to decide where to apply. Under the stated preferences, data science and operations research are starting points. Shared economics training does not make the categories identical—or establish that either is the best path for every graduate.






NoteSources, scraping, and replication





The six archived Summary HTML fragments were captured September 20, 2026. Pay refers to May 2025; projections cover 2025-2035. The original capture method and file hashes are recorded in data/raw/manifest.csv. The numerical inputs are extracted from those HTML files with rvest, not manually copied into the comparison table.

# Collect structured information from BLS HTML using rvest.
# Run from the project root. Archived HTML makes the default run reproducible.
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(rvest)
  library(dplyr)
  library(stringr)
  library(readr)
})

sources <- tibble::tribble(
  ~id, ~occupation, ~path,
  "data-scientists", "Data scientists", "math/data-scientists.htm",
  "economists", "Economists", "life-physical-and-social-science/economists.htm",
  "operations-research-analysts", "Operations research analysts", "math/operations-research-analysts.htm",
  "market-research-analysts", "Market research analysts", "business-and-financial/market-research-analysts.htm",
  "management-analysts", "Management analysts", "business-and-financial/management-analysts.htm",
  "financial-analysts", "Financial analysts", "business-and-financial/financial-analysts.htm"
) |>
  mutate(url = paste0("https://www.bls.gov/ooh/", path))

scrape_profile <- function(file, id, occupation, url) {
  page <- read_html(file, encoding = "UTF-8")
  rows <- html_elements(page, "#quickfacts tbody tr")
  if (length(rows) != 7L) stop("Quick Facts structure changed: ", file)
  fields <- tibble::tibble(
    label = str_squish(html_text2(html_element(rows, "th"))),
    value = str_squish(html_text2(html_element(rows, "td")))
  )
  get_field <- function(pattern) {
    value <- fields$value[str_detect(fields$label, regex(pattern, ignore_case = TRUE))]
    if (length(value) != 1L || is.na(value) || value == "") {
      stop("Missing or ambiguous field: ", pattern, " in ", file)
    }
    value
  }
  # Scope to the Summary article, so the same sentence elsewhere is not counted twice.
  summary <- html_element(page, "article[aria-labelledby='Summary']")
  if (is.na(html_name(summary))) stop("Summary article missing: ", file)
  body <- str_squish(html_text2(summary))
  openings <- str_match(body, "About\\s+([0-9,]+)\\s+openings")[, 2]
  period <- str_match(body, "from\\s+(20[0-9]{2})\\s+to\\s+(20[0-9]{2})")
  pay_label <- fields$label[str_detect(fields$label, "Median Pay")]
  pay_text <- get_field("Median Pay")
  result <- tibble::tibble(
    id, occupation, source_url = url,
    # Annual pay is the FIRST amount; the hourly amount is deliberately excluded.
    median_pay_usd = parse_number(pay_text),
    pay_year = as.integer(str_extract(pay_label, "20[0-9]{2}")),
    education = get_field("Entry-Level Education"),
    experience = get_field("Work Experience"),
    employment = parse_number(get_field("Number of Jobs")),
    growth_pct = parse_number(get_field("Job Outlook")),
    net_new_jobs = parse_number(get_field("Employment Change")),
    annual_openings = parse_number(openings),
    projection_start = as.integer(period[, 2]),
    projection_end = as.integer(period[, 3])
  )
  if (anyNA(result)) stop("A required field could not be parsed: ", file)
  result
}

collect_data <- function(raw_dir = "data/raw") {
  manifest <- read_csv(file.path(raw_dir, "manifest.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  if (anyDuplicated(manifest$id) || !setequal(manifest$id, sources$id)) {
    stop("Manifest must contain exactly one record for each source.")
  }
  files <- file.path(raw_dir, paste0(manifest$id, ".html"))
  if (!all(file.exists(files))) stop("An archived HTML file is missing.")
  if ("md5" %in% names(manifest) &&
      !all(unname(tools::md5sum(files)) == manifest$md5)) {
    stop("Archived HTML differs from its manifest. Review the inputs before analysis.")
  }
  data <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(sources)), function(i) {
    s <- sources[i, ]
    scrape_profile(file.path(raw_dir, paste0(s$id, ".html")),
                   s$id, s$occupation, s$url)
  })) |>
    left_join(select(manifest, id, access_date, capture_method), by = "id")
  stopifnot(nrow(data) == 6L, !anyDuplicated(data$id), !anyNA(data),
            all(data$median_pay_usd > 0), all(data$annual_openings > 0),
            all(data$employment > 0), all(data$projection_end > data$projection_start),
            length(unique(data$pay_year)) == 1L,
            length(unique(data$projection_start)) == 1L,
            length(unique(data$projection_end)) == 1L)
  # All monetary figures must refer to the same year for meaningful comparisons.
  dir.create("data/processed", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  write_csv(data, "data/processed/careers.csv")
  data
}

# OPTIONAL live collection. The supplied report uses the archived September 2026
# snapshot. New data go to a separate directory, preserving that original evidence.
refresh_sources <- function(destination = "data/live") {
  if (!requireNamespace("httr2", quietly = TRUE)) stop("Install httr2 first.")
  if (dir.exists(destination)) stop("Use a new destination to preserve earlier data.")
  ua <- "EconomicsCourseProject/1.0 (six public BLS career pages; educational use)"
  get_public <- function(url) {
    httr2::request(url) |>
      httr2::req_user_agent(ua) |>
      httr2::req_timeout(30) |>
      httr2::req_perform()  # Stops on HTTP errors, including 403 and 429. No retries.
  }
  robots <- httr2::resp_body_string(get_public("https://www.bls.gov/robots.txt"))
  if (!grepl("User-agent:", robots, ignore.case = TRUE)) stop("Cannot verify robots.txt.")
  # Conservative check: honor Disallow rules from ALL groups, ignore Allow
  # exceptions, and stop if any rule could exclude one of these six paths.
  # This intentionally may refuse more than necessary; it never tries to evade a rule.
  lines <- trimws(gsub("#.*$", "", strsplit(robots, "\n", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]))
  rules <- trimws(sub("^[Dd]isallow\\s*:", "", lines[grepl("^[Dd]isallow\\s*:", lines)]))
  rules <- rules[nzchar(rules)]
  url_paths <- sub("https://www.bls.gov", "", sources$url, fixed = TRUE)
  for (rule in rules) {
    # Convert robots wildcards to a regular expression. Unanchored rules
    # match prefixes; a terminal $ requires a match through the end of a path.
    pattern <- glob2rx(sub("\\$$", "", rule), trim.head = FALSE, trim.tail = FALSE)
    if (!endsWith(rule, "$")) pattern <- sub("\\$$", "", pattern)
    if (any(grepl(pattern, url_paths))) {
      stop("A robots.txt rule may disallow these pages: ", rule,
           ". Stop and review the site's policy; do not bypass it.")
    }
  }
  delay <- 3
  crawl <- lines[grepl("^Crawl-delay:", lines, ignore.case = TRUE)]
  if (length(crawl)) delay <- max(delay, parse_number(crawl), na.rm = TRUE)
  dir.create(destination, recursive = TRUE)
  writeLines(robots, file.path(destination, "robots.txt"))
  manifest <- list()
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(sources))) {
    Sys.sleep(delay)
    s <- sources[i, ]
    response <- get_public(s$url)
    content <- httr2::resp_body_raw(response)
    file <- file.path(destination, paste0(s$id, ".html"))
    writeBin(content, file)
    # rvest collects and validates the relevant fields immediately after download.
    scrape_profile(file, s$id, s$occupation, s$url)
    manifest[[i]] <- tibble::tibble(id = s$id, source_url = s$url,
      access_date = as.character(Sys.Date()), capture_method = "HTTP download; rvest extraction")
    write_csv(bind_rows(manifest), file.path(destination, "manifest.csv"))
  }
  message("Saved six pages. Run collect_data(raw_dir = '", destination, "') and analyze_careers() to review them.")
  invisible(destination)
}

title: Florida and South Carolina: Two Different Growth Stories
text:
Florida added 196,680 residents between July 2024 and July 2025. South Carolina added 79,958. Which population flows account for those gains, and how do their contributions differ across states?
The Census estimates give different answers. South Carolina’s growth was mainly a domestic-migration story; Florida’s largest contribution came from net international migration. Mapping the two measures separately shows why “a growing state” is too broad a label for understanding demographic change.
This matters for economic planning. More residents can mean more demand for homes, transportation, and services. But total growth alone cannot tell a community which demographic flows it needs to understand.

title: Florida and South Carolina: Two Different Growth Stories
section: First, put growth on a comparable scale
text:
First, put growth on a comparable scale
I join the Census Bureau’s Vintage 2025 population estimates to official state polygons using two-digit state FIPS identifiers. The analysis covers all 50 states. Maps show the contiguous 48; Alaska and Hawaii remain in the downloadable comparison. Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico are excluded from this state comparison.
Raw counts favor large states. Instead, each map expresses change per 1,000 residents, using the average of the July 2024 and July 2025 populations. A value of 10 means a gain equivalent to 10 people for every 1,000 residents. Both maps use identical colors and limits, so their shades are directly comparable.





Annual population change per 1,000 residents. Selected states are labeled; all 50 states appear in the saved comparison. Boundaries are generalized Census polygons in an equal-area projection.




South Carolina leads at 14.5 additional residents per 1,000, with Idaho close behind at 14.3. Florida gains 8.4. Parts of the South and Mountain West stand out, but a color indicating growth does not identify its source.

title: Florida and South Carolina: Two Different Growth Stories
text:
Now map domestic migration
Domestic migration is arrivals from elsewhere in the United States minus departures to other U.S. locations. It is a net balance, not the number of people who moved in. A state can have many arrivals and departures at the same time.





Net domestic migration per 1,000 residents. The color scale matches the first map. Differences between the maps reflect the other components of population change.




South Carolina remains dark teal: its domestic gain is 12.0 per 1,000 residents. Florida becomes much lighter, at only 1.0. Similar growth colors on the first map can therefore conceal quite different migration balances.
The distinction also matters outside the South. 15 of the 50 states grew despite net domestic outflows. Pennsylvania, for example, gained 1.0 residents per 1,000 overall while losing 0.2 through domestic migration. Calling it simply a state people are “leaving” would miss the rest of its population balance.

title: Florida and South Carolina: Two Different Growth Stories
text:
What fills the gap?
Population change combines net domestic migration, net international migration, births minus deaths, and a small Census reconciliation adjustment. These components classify flows; they are not mutually exclusive groups of people. “International” is a geographic category, not a citizenship or visa category; it also includes returning U.S.-born residents and other movements covered by the Census definition.





Four illustrative states chosen to contrast demographic balances. Positive bars extend right and negative bars left; the diamond marks their signed sum. Small residual adjustments are retained.




Florida’s net international gain was 178,674, compared with a domestic gain of 22,517. In Pennsylvania, international migration more than offset both domestic outflows and deaths exceeding births. California shows the reverse outcome: births exceeding deaths and international migration nearly offset its domestic loss, but its estimated population still edged down.
These are one-year accounting contributions, not proof of why people chose a destination. The figures do not establish effects of taxes, housing costs, jobs, or state policies. Nor do they reveal migrants’ ages, occupations, or service needs. State averages also conceal differences between cities and rural areas. The estimates may be revised; a small one-year change does not establish a lasting trend.
The takeaway: locate where population grew or declined, then examine the components before explaining the pattern. Domestic migration was central to South Carolina’s gain, while international migration contributed most to Florida’s. These balances provide a starting point for local planning; identifying particular housing or service needs requires additional local and demographic data.






NoteData, GIS methods, and replication





Population: NST-EST2025-ALLDATA, released January 2026; variable definitions and methodology. The analysis isolates July 2024-July 2025 using one consistent vintage, not a mixture of releases. These are published population estimates, not an unweighted microdata sample.
Geography: Census TIGERweb Generalized ACS 2024 State/County service, States 20M layer. The public service supplies generalized polygon coordinates transformed to EPSG:5070, NAD83 / Conus Albers, an equal-area projection for the contiguous United States. R draws those cached projected coordinates with ggplot2; no local GIS system libraries are required. The 2024 outline vintage is separate from the 2025 population-estimate vintage.
All inputs were downloaded October 17, 2026. Exact URLs and hashes are in data/raw/manifest.csv. The code verifies 50 unique state matches, agreement of state names, 48 mapped states, valid coordinates, and exact reconciliation of the population components. Polygon vertex order and separate rings are preserved; joins use FIPS codes rather than names.
Raw files are included, so rendering does not contact either data service. R/download_data.R reproduces acquisition to a separate folder if needed. Numeric statements, figures, join checks, tables, and comparison files are generated by R. The Post 5 README gives replication and publishing instructions.

# Read the included official Census files. Never download during rendering.
prepare_data <- function() {
  manifest <- read.csv("data/raw/manifest.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  files <- file.path("data/raw", manifest$file)
  if (!all(file.exists(files))) stop("Keep the complete data/raw folder with the post.")
  if (!all(unname(tools::md5sum(files)) == manifest$md5)) {
    stop("An input file changed. Review its provenance before using it.")
  }
  pop <- read.csv("data/raw/population_2025.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  # 040 = state-level records. Analyze 50 states; exclude DC and Puerto Rico.
  pop <- pop[pop$SUMLEV == 40 & !pop$STATE %in% c(11, 72), ]
  stopifnot(nrow(pop) == 50, !anyDuplicated(pop$STATE))
  d <- data.frame(
    fips = sprintf("%02d", pop$STATE), state = pop$NAME,
    population_2024 = pop$POPESTIMATE2024,
    population_2025 = pop$POPESTIMATE2025,
    population_change = pop$NPOPCHG_2025,
    domestic = pop$DOMESTICMIG2025,
    international = pop$INTERNATIONALMIG2025,
    natural = pop$NATURALCHG2025,
    residual = pop$RESIDUAL2025,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  # Use a common average-population denominator so component rates add exactly.
  d$average_population <- (d$population_2024 + d$population_2025) / 2
  for (name in c("population_change", "domestic", "international", "natural", "residual")) {
    d[[paste0(name, "_rate")]] <- 1000 * d[[name]] / d$average_population
  }
  stopifnot(!anyNA(d), all(d$average_population > 0),
    all(d$population_2025 - d$population_2024 == d$population_change),
    all(d$domestic + d$international + d$natural + d$residual == d$population_change),
    max(abs(d$domestic_rate - pop$RDOMESTICMIG2025)) < 0.000001)

  # ESRI JSON polygons are already projected by the Census service into meters.
  # Read coordinate rings directly; sf/GDAL/PROJ are not needed on the laptop.
  geo <- jsonlite::fromJSON("data/raw/states_2024_albers.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
  stopifnot(geo$spatialReference$wkid == 5070,
            !isTRUE(geo$exceededTransferLimit))
  points <- list()
  keys <- list()
  n <- 0L
  for (feature in geo$features) {
    id <- feature$attributes$GEOID
    if (!id %in% d$fips) next
    keys[[length(keys) + 1L]] <- data.frame(fips = id,
      boundary_state = feature$attributes$NAME,
      abbreviation = feature$attributes$STUSAB)
    for (r in seq_along(feature$geometry$rings)) {
      xy <- do.call(rbind, lapply(feature$geometry$rings[[r]], unlist))
      n <- n + 1L
      points[[n]] <- data.frame(fips = id, ring = paste(id, r, sep = "_"),
        vertex = seq_len(nrow(xy)), x = xy[, 1], y = xy[, 2])
    }
  }
  points <- do.call(rbind, points)
  keys <- do.call(rbind, keys)
  stopifnot(nrow(keys) == 50, !anyDuplicated(keys$fips),
            setequal(d$fips, keys$fips), all(is.finite(points$x)), all(is.finite(points$y)))
  d <- merge(d, keys, by = "fips", sort = FALSE)
  stopifnot(all(d$state == d$boundary_state))
  # Preserve original vertex order: a sorting join can corrupt polygon shapes.
  map <- cbind(points, d[match(points$fips, d$fips), setdiff(names(d), "fips")])
  rownames(map) <- NULL
  map <- map[!map$fips %in% c("02", "15"), ]
  stopifnot(length(unique(map$fips)) == 48, !anyNA(map))
  audit <- data.frame(fips = d$fips, state = d$state,
    boundary_match = TRUE, mapped_in_lower48 = !d$fips %in% c("02", "15"))
  dir.create("data/processed", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  write.csv(d, "data/processed/state_rates.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  write.csv(map, "data/processed/map_vertices.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  write.csv(audit, "results/join_audit.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  list(states = d, map = map)
}

      ggplot2::coord_fixed() +

title: One Family Link, Several Measures of Income Persistence
text:
Does measured income persistence change when we replace one year’s income with several years—and measure the child later in life? That question matters when interpreting economic mobility: a student’s first job may say little about their eventual earnings.
This tutorial links real mothers and children, then compares income definitions on the same 356 children from 290 mothers. The single-year elasticity is 0.017; averaging both generations gives 0.084. The uncertainty is wide, so these are measurement comparisons, not a precise estimate of U.S. mobility.

title: One Family Link, Several Measures of Income Persistence
text:
1. Start with documented family links
I use the BLS NLSY79 and Children/Young Adult public-use files, the archived releases through the 2018 wave. BLS documents the link: child ID C00001.00 identifies the individual; C00002.00 identifies their mother and groups maternal siblings. It matches the mother’s R00001.00 in NLSY79. I call this maternal-family key family_id; it does not identify a current household.
Download the repository folder, open a Terminal inside blog/posts/post6, and run:
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python code/run_analysis.py
Python reshapes the supplied original-variable extracts into person-year tables and loads SQLite, using Python’s built-in sqlite3 module. No database server is needed. The complete pipeline saves its database and results. To follow individual steps in a Python session opened in this folder:
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "code")
from run_analysis import build_database, fit_ige

con, matched, sample_flow = build_database()

# Run a SQL query from Python and inspect five actual matches.
import pandas as pd
print(pd.read_sql_query("""
    SELECT child_id, family_id, mother_id
    FROM links ORDER BY child_id LIMIT 5
""", con))
The actual matching query is:
-- C00002.00 is the mother's NLSY79 ID. It also groups maternal siblings.
-- SELECT chooses the columns; JOIN matches this family key to one mother.
CREATE TABLE links AS
SELECT c.child_id, c.family_id, m.mother_id,
       c.birth_year AS child_birth_year, c.sex AS child_sex,
       m.birth_year AS mother_birth_year
FROM children AS c
JOIN mothers AS m ON c.family_id = m.mother_id
WHERE m.sex = 2 AND m.sample_code BETWEEN 5 AND 8;

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX links_child_key ON links(child_id);
SELECT chooses columns. JOIN ... ON attaches each child to the mother with the matching identifier. WHERE restricts mothers to the original cross-sectional sample. Multiple children can match one mother; each child must appear once. A unique index checks that rule.

title: One Family Link, Several Measures of Income Persistence
text:
2. Build comparable income measures
Here, income means the individual’s annual wages, salary, commissions and tips before tax, excluding self-employment and other income. Parental income is maternal earnings; it does not combine both parents’ resources.
The script converts negative missing-data codes to missing values and adjusts earnings to 2018 dollars using annual CPI-U, before averaging. Age means income year minus birth year. From the 2014 child wave onward, income year follows the actual interview date.
-- GROUP BY collapses person-year rows to one row per person.
-- AVG aggregates wage LEVELS (including zeros); COUNT records coverage.
-- WHERE filters input rows; HAVING filters the resulting groups.
CREATE TABLE parent_average AS
SELECT mother_id, AVG(real_wages) AS parent_average,
       COUNT(*) AS parent_years
FROM mother_real
WHERE age BETWEEN 35 AND 40
GROUP BY mother_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;

CREATE TABLE child_early_average AS
SELECT child_id, AVG(real_wages) AS early_average,
       COUNT(*) AS early_years
FROM child_real
WHERE age BETWEEN 20 AND 25
GROUP BY child_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;

CREATE TABLE child_mature_average AS
SELECT child_id, AVG(real_wages) AS mature_average,
       COUNT(*) AS mature_years
FROM child_real
WHERE age BETWEEN 30 AND 39
GROUP BY child_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;
GROUP BY collects each person’s rows. Aggregation reduces them to a summary: AVG calculates mean real earnings; COUNT records coverage. HAVING requires enough observed years. Zeros remain in these averages; missing years do not become zeros. Older children were interviewed less frequently, so these are averages of observed annual incomes, not complete annual histories.
For single-year measures, the code selects observations closest to maternal age 38 and child ages 23 and 35, breaking ties toward the earlier year. It selects the year before checking whether income is positive. All comparisons then use the same pairs with positive anchor incomes and averages. Aggregate each annual panel first, then join the summaries; joining both annual panels directly would multiply rows.

title: One Family Link, Several Measures of Income Persistence
text:
3. Estimate and interpret the IGE
The intergenerational elasticity is the slope in
\[
\log(Y_{child,i})=\alpha+\beta\log(Y_{mother,i})+\varepsilon_i.
\]
It describes proportional differences, not dollars inherited or a causal effect. For small differences, 1% higher maternal earnings is associated with approximately \(\beta\)% higher child earnings. Python estimates the slope by ordinary least squares:
import numpy as np

x = np.log(matched["parent_average"].to_numpy())
y = np.log(matched["mature_average"].to_numpy())
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x])
alpha, ige = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]
print(ige)

# Same slope, with uncertainty accounting for siblings sharing a mother:
print(fit_ige(matched, "parent_average", "mature_average"))



Three estimates using the same children: one income year in both generations, average maternal income with one child year, and averages in both generations. All confidence intervals include zero.


Averaging maternal income raises the point estimate to 0.098; averaging the child’s income as well gives 0.084. Averaging need not raise the estimate at every step. The paired cluster-bootstrap interval for the overall change includes zero. These data do not establish a statistically clear increase.

title: One Family Link, Several Measures of Income Persistence
text:
4. Separate averaging from life-cycle timing



With the same maternal income average and the same children, early and later single-year estimates differ. Averaged child-income estimates are closer, but confidence intervals are wide.


Holding maternal income fixed, the single-child-year estimate changes from 0.012 in the early-career window to 0.098 in the thirties. The paired difference is imprecise. This demonstrates age sensitivity, a warning sign of life-cycle bias; it cannot reveal the exact bias without lifetime income.
Why can bias arise? Suppose early log earnings equal \(\lambda_a\) times long-run log earnings, plus unrelated noise. With an accurate parental measure, the observed slope is approximately \(\beta_a=\lambda_a\beta_{\text{long run}}\). If \(\lambda_a<1\), an early snapshot understates persistence. Different career growth paths make this possible; simply adding an average age profile does not fix it (Haider and Solon, 2006).
Averaging can reduce temporary shocks and reporting noise. Independent yearly shocks average out; persistent shocks average out more slowly. Averaging early-career income still cannot guarantee a measure of lifetime status.



Eight maternal-income groups show an uneven relationship with adult-child average earnings, reinforcing the uncertainty in the estimated elasticity.


These unweighted estimates describe a selected, observed sample, not the U.S. population. Attrition, young motherhood in older child cohorts, positive-income restrictions, top coding, gender differences and calendar conditions limit interpretation. Lifetime income is unobserved; the later average is a benchmark, not ground truth.
The takeaway: establish the family link, average comparable real incomes, and check measurement ages before interpreting an IGE as persistence in long-run economic status. A successful SQL match solves identification of relatives; economic interpretation still depends on what their income measures capture.
